blocks.text: Digestion turns the food you eat into molecules small enough to pass into your **blood**. It happens in two ways at once: *mechanical* and *chemical*.
Remember the order with the phrase **Many Old Stories Start Long ago**: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

blocks.title: The journey of a bite of food

items.title: Mouth
items.text: Teeth break food apart and saliva starts digesting starch.

items.title: Oesophagus
items.text: Waves of muscle called *peristalsis* push food down.

items.title: Stomach
items.text: Acid and pepsin turn food into a thick liquid called chyme.

items.title: Small intestine
items.text: Enzymes finish the job and villi absorb the nutrients.

items.title: Large intestine
items.text: Water is taken back and the rest leaves the body.

blocks.definition: A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

rows.label: What it does
values: Breaks large molecules into small ones

blocks.text: Amylase in saliva and from the pancreas breaks starch into sugars such as glucose.
Pepsin starts in the stomach; pancreatic enzymes finish the job, leaving amino acids.
Bile emulsifies fat, then lipase splits it into fatty acids and glycerol.

items.label: 2–4 h
items.title: Leaving the stomach
items.text: Chyme moves into the small intestine.

items.label: ≈ 6 h
items.title: Absorption done
items.text: Most nutrients are in the blood.

items.title: Why does the stomach not digest itself?

blocks.text: A thick layer of mucus protects its lining from acid and pepsin.

items.title: What does the rate of reaction depend on?

blocks.text: Enzyme speed follows temperature and pH, e.g. pepsin works best near $pH \approx 2$.

blocks.caption: A toy model of the journey

points: Mechanical digestion makes pieces smaller; chemical digestion makes molecules smaller.
Most absorption happens in the small intestine, through the villi.
